patterns.name: Back-dated MTM valuations for counterparty audit requests
patterns.summary: Counterparties' auditors need third-party valuations of their derivatives, and the Confirmations group (Larry Joe Hunter, Ellen Wallumrod) must supply them. Confirmations has no system that values deals, so each request is emailed to every Risk desk head (5 or 6 of them). Each desk head forwards it to an analyst, who pulls a mini-book for that counterparty as of a past date, exports it to Excel, blacks out sensitive columns (Delta/Vol) and replies. Confirmations then combines the desk replies. Hunter says requests come several times a week.

observations.quote: We do not have access to any system that values these deals, but are looking to get the on-line "EnTelligence" built so that it carries back-dated curves that will allow us to complete these requests without taking up a Risk person's time and without having to black out information (Delta/Vol) that is included in a mini-book.
observations.note: Confirmations itself says the work takes Risk staff time, includes blacking out Delta/Vol, and would go away with a back-dated valuation tool.

observations.quote: Until we can get EnTelligence built to our specifications, we'll need to continue to go to the different desks to provide Mark-to-Market valuations for a Counterparty's portfolio.

patterns.name: Weekly manual compaction of WeaponX Access databases
patterns.summary: WeaponX is an Access database that imports and deletes a lot of data every day, and Access does not free the space, so the files grow (one went from 520 MB to 30 MB when compacted). Greg Couch asked every book admin who uses WeaponX, across six managers' groups, to compact their file by hand at least once a week: open it holding the shift key, run Tools/Database Utilities/Compact Database, wait for it to finish, then use it as normal. One admin already does this every day.

occurrences.quote: I would like each of your book admins using WeaponX to begin using the following procedures at least once/week (if they aren't already).
Try this and see if it does any good.

observations.quote: Open the database while holding down on the shift key. This will open the database, but prevent the main form from opening automatically. Next, the admin should go to Access menu selections and choose Tools/Database Utilities/Compact Database.
observations.note: The manual steps each admin repeats: open the file a special way, run compact from the menus, wait for it to finish, and reopen.

observations.quote: WeaponX imports and deletes a lot of data on a daily basis.
observations.note: The files grow every day, so compaction is a standing chore, not a one-off.

observations.quote: The Texas WeaponX file that I compacted reduced from 520 MB to 30 MB and one for the west went from 400 MB to 12 MB.
observations.note: Files of hundreds of MB take a while to compact, which is time the admin spends waiting.

patterns.name: Monthly roll of Sitara transport usage tickets
patterns.summary: Before each new month Heidi Withers (rates group) goes through the HPL and third-party transport usage tickets in Sitara one by one, adds the new month where needed and refreshes each rate by hand to match the rate matrix. When she adds a month she leaves the volume at zero, so the schedulers on Daren Farmer's desk must fill in volumes and are told to check every pipe. The correct rates already sit in Unify for invoicing, so the Sitara tickets are a second, hand-kept copy, and mismatches with the matrix have been found.

She asks each of them to search all their books for deals that settle between ECC and an outside counterparty and move ('flip') them to the FT-US/CAND-ERMS book, usually by end of day. Darron Giron forwards each request to 5 to 7 book administrators, who check their own books. EnronOnline deals land in Houston books automatically, so the mistake comes back every month. patterns.name: Extending Sitara deals for meter flow outside the deal term

A Volume Management analyst (Fred Boas, Aimee Lannou, Jackie Young) looks up the last deal and emails the desk lead, Daren Farmer, one meter at a time, asking him to extend the deal or create a new one. patterns.name: Monthly P&L top pages for Arthur Andersen's gas testing
patterns.summary: Each month the auditors from Arthur Andersen (Mark Austin, Sharon Smith, Carrie Richardson) email the gas Risk desk heads (Kelly, Keiser, Giron, Baumbach) a list of books. For each book they want the P&L top page for the last day of the month. If most of the P&L comes from curve shift, they also want the top pages and curve shift reports for the five largest days. Each desk head forwards the email to two to seven book admins. The admins pull the reports from ERMS and print or copy them, and the desk head passes them on to the auditors. The auditors chase missing books ('2nd request', quarter-file close-out) and ask who is responsible for each desk.

patterns.name: Monthly wholesale-volume variance explanations for Investor Relations
patterns.summary: Each month Business Analysis & Reporting (Misti Day) emails about 11 commercial contacts to open the "Statistical Database", review their region's wholesale volumes for the month, and email back a verification plus a written explanation for every change of 10% or more year/year, quarter/quarter and month/month, by a deadline a few days later. Each person finds their flagged lines, works out the cause and types a free-text reply. BA&R then gathers the separate email replies for Investor Relations. The causes often carry over from month to month: in June and September the Texas reply gave the same reasons (more EOL trading and Entex taking more gas).

patterns.name: Nightly check that every post ID is officialized
patterns.summary: Each night the gas book administrators must officialize every post ID (book) so the V@R and credit systems pick it up. Since October 2000, after a missed West-NW-GDL book put the desk on Risk's daily list of non-officialized books (sent to Sally Beck and reviewed weekly by Rick Buy), one person per desk group runs an Excel macro by hand: they enter the date and the Portfolio and Book codes, and the macro lists the books that are officialized. The groups led by Gossett, Baumbach, Kelly, Giron and Keiser each got this file, and staff pass round changed versions of it. Regional controllers also get an end-of-night sheet confirming all books are officialized, and Risk keeps its own daily list of misses. No system holds the full list of books each admin must officialize, so Darron Giron writes it out by hand when another group asks (Rahmaan in July, Connie Sutton and Susan Trevino in November 2000). The check used before the macro compared positions only, so it missed post IDs with no net position. Credit needs those flat books officialized too.

We have been tracking books that are not officialized on a daily basis.

Darron forwards the request to his analyst, Patrick Ryder, who pulls the deal detail and either saves it to the ERMS/1Intra/FRED Liquidations folder or emails it to Jim. The director then sends the combined file back, and assistants such as Irena Hogan forward it again. That survey also drives each cost center's costs to the commercial teams and asks them to confirm or change the percentage given to each team. patterns.name: Weekly check that new ERMS curves exist in RisktRAC
patterns.summary: When a trader needs a new price curve, the commodity group's risk management builds it in ERMS. They then fill in a curve set-up form so that Risk Analysis and Reporting can set it up again in RisktRAC, the system that calculates VaR. Separately, they email IT to add the curve to TAGG. Desks have not always sent the form, so Risk Analysis and Reporting now checks by hand every week that all curves newly set up in ERMS are also in RisktRAC. The first check found numerous curves missing, and each has to be resolved with the desk. Until a curve is in RisktRAC, its positions are left out of VaR, so VaR is wrong.

observations.note: The weekly check turns up many missing curves, and each one is then followed up with the desk.

observations.quote: If the curve is not set up in RisktRAC the positions are not captured in the VAR or engine, thereby making VAR inaccurate.
observations.note: Why the gap matters: a curve missing from RisktRAC leaves its positions out of VaR until someone finds it.

observations.quote: In the past few months, the procedures for setting up new curves and books have not been followed by everyone.
observations.note: The hand-completed form is not reliably sent, which is why the weekly check was started.

This repeats on the roll-off nights until indexes are set, and the procedure is complex enough that desk leads planned classroom training on it.

observations.note: The roll-off covers at least two nights, so the double calc is done on each of them.

patterns.name: Nightly El Paso Electric model-vs-CARP tie-out
patterns.summary: On the Portland Real Time desk, the shift trader who markets El Paso Electric (EPE) must, when the trading day is done, tie out the El Paso model spreadsheet against the CARP report by eye, then log the El Paso totals in a separate monthly EPE reconciliation workbook and explain every variance. The sheet must be filled in even when nothing differs, because Houston takes an empty sheet to mean the CARP was not run. Traders sometimes skip it. Differences that are not caught surface at the monthly checkout with El Paso and Settlements; the June 2001 checkout took five days to sort out.
